warmup.q: class FrontDesk(var printer: Printer) : Printer by printer. You build it with Laser("laser-1"), then set desk.printer = Laser("laser-2"). Which printer does desk.print("flyer.pdf") use?
options: laser-2, because by printer forwards to the property
laser-1, because the delegate was stored when the object was built
It doesn't compile: a var can't be a delegate
It throws, because the delegate changed under it
warmup.why: The compiler copies the constructor argument into a hidden private final Printer $$delegate_0 field, and the generated print calls that field. Assigning printer changes the property only. It compiles without a warning, which is why the first option catches people. The first section shows both fields in javap.

opening:
At the print shop's front counter, a clerk takes your questions. She answers a few herself and passes the rest to the expert in the back room, so you never need to know who that is. Next to the counter is a cloakroom. You hand in your coat and get a ticket; later you hand back the ticket, and the attendant fetches the coat. Both are delegation: you ask one person, and someone else does the work.

Kotlin has both kinds under one keyword, by. Class delegation is the clerk: a class passes calls on to another object. A delegated property is the cloakroom: reading or writing the property goes through a helper object. The trap is in the clerk's notebook. She wrote down the expert's name on her first day, in ink, and changing the name on the door doesn't change whom she asks.

In the last lesson, the compiler erased a wrapper class. This time it writes wrappers for us. We'll find the hidden field behind class delegation, open up a delegated property, put a price on by lazy, and try the standard delegates. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the front counter and the cloakroom. Class delegation is the clerk: every call she doesn't answer herself goes to the expert she wrote down on day one. A delegated property is the ticket: a hidden field holds the attendant, and the getter and setter just hand over the ticket.

In your own code, search for by lazy in classes you create many times, and for a var constructor parameter used after by. The first is a bill, the second a swap that never happens.

Next, we'll give a lambda a receiver, an object it runs inside, so its code can call a builder's functions without naming it. How do plain functions add up to a small language?

sections.h: Class delegation: every call goes to the object you passed in, captured once
sections.html:
An interface lists methods without saying how they work, and a class that implements it fills them in. The print shop's app has one for its printers, Printer, with a print(document) method, and a Laser class that implements it.

To wrap such a class, you write a new class that implements the same interface and forwards each call to the wrapped object, changing only the behavior you care about. That's the Decorator pattern, which lesson 5 of the patterns track built by hand. Kotlin writes the forwarding for you.

In class FrontDesk(var printer: Printer) : Printer by printer, the part by printer is class delegation. The compiler writes every method of Printer as a call on printer, except the ones you write yourself. In the print shop, FrontDesk is the clerk at the counter, and the Laser is the expert in the back room. You ask the clerk, and the expert does the work.

Two details matter once you put by into real classes. The first is that the delegate is captured once. by printer looks as if it forwards to the printer property, but javap shows two fields:

private final Printer $$delegate_0;   // set from the constructor argument, never changed
private Printer printer;              // the property you can reassign

The generated print calls $$delegate_0. Assign a new printer, and the property changes, but every call still goes to the old one. The demo prints after swap, printer = Laser(laser-2): flyer.pdf printed on laser-1. That's the clerk's notebook: she wrote the expert's name down on her first day, in ink.

A hand-written Java decorator reads its field on every call, so swapping works there:

Java
final class FrontDeskJava implements Printer {
    private Printer printer;
    FrontDeskJava(Printer printer) { this.printer = printer; }
    void setPrinter(Printer printer) { this.printer = printer; }

    @Override public String print(String document) {
        return printer.print(document);            // the current field, on every call
    }
}
Kotlin
class FrontDesk(var printer: Printer) : Printer by printer   // forwards to the FIRST printer

val desk = FrontDesk(Laser("laser-1"))
desk.printer = Laser("laser-2")
desk.print("flyer.pdf")   // "flyer.pdf printed on laser-1": $$delegate_0 still holds laser-1

If the target has to change while the program runs, write the forwarding yourself. Otherwise make the constructor parameter a plain parameter or a val, so nobody expects it to move.

by captures the delegate once, when the object is built. If the target must change, write the forwarding yourself.

The second detail: equals, hashCode and toString are not forwarded. They come from Any, the root of every Kotlin class, not from the interface. Ask the clerk who she is, and she talks about herself, not the expert.

The demo's Tags class delegates MutableSet<String> to an inner set. It prints as workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.Tags@2d209079, a name only a hash function could love, and two Tags with the same elements are not equal. That breaks the contract of Set, which says two sets with the same elements are equal, and a HashSet<Tags> will happily keep both. Override the three, and forward them to the inner set, when the wrapper should behave like what it wraps.

With those two details in mind, by is still the best tool for one job: wrapping a wide interface to change one or two methods. Take java.sql.Connection, the JDK's interface for a connection to a database, which has dozens of methods. A wrapper that logs each close() needs one override, and the compiler writes all the others, so none of them can be forgotten.

The same keyword does a different job on a property, and it compiles to something quite different.

code.title: ClassDelegationDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo interface Printer { fun print(document: String): String } class Laser(private val name: String) : Printer { override fun print(document: String): String = "$document printed on $name" override fun toString(): String = "Laser($name)" } /** `by printer` forwards to the object passed in at construction, stored in a hidden final field. */ class FrontDesk(var printer: Printer) : Printer by printer /** Delegating a Set forwards Set's methods, but not equals, hashCode or toString. */ class Tags(private val inner: MutableSet<String> = HashSet()) : MutableSet<String> by inner fun main() { val desk = FrontDesk(Laser("laser-1")) println(desk.print("flyer.pdf")) desk.printer = Laser("laser-2") // swap the printer... println("after swap, printer = ${desk.printer}: ${desk.print("flyer.pdf")}") val a = Tags().apply { add("rush"); add("colour") } val b = Tags().apply { add("rush"); add("colour") } println("a = $a") println("a == b: ${a == b}, a.size = ${a.size}, \"rush\" in a: ${"rush" in a}") }

alt.title: ClassDelegationDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; /** * Java twin of ClassDelegationDemo.kt. Java has no `by`, so you write the forwarding yourself. * Written by hand, it reads the field on every call, so swapping the printer works. */ public class ClassDelegationDemoJava { static final class FrontDeskJava implements Printer { private Printer printer; FrontDeskJava(Printer printer) { this.printer = printer; } void setPrinter(Printer printer) { this.printer = printer; } @Override public String print(String document) { return printer.print(document); // reads the current field each time } } public static void main(String[] args) { FrontDeskJava desk = new FrontDeskJava(new Laser("laser-1")); System.out.println(desk.print("flyer.pdf")); desk.setPrinter(new Laser("laser-2")); System.out.println("after swap: " + desk.print("flyer.pdf")); // the Kotlin class, seen from Java: setPrinter changes the property, not the $$delegate_0 field FrontDesk kotlinDesk = new FrontDesk(new Laser("laser-1")); kotlinDesk.setPrinter(new Laser("laser-2")); System.out.println("Kotlin class after swap: " + kotlinDesk.print("flyer.pdf")); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints flyer.pdf printed on laser-1, then after swap, printer = Laser(laser-2): flyer.pdf printed on laser-1: the property moved, the calls didn't. javap lists private final ...Printer $$delegate_0 and private ...Printer printer. The Java decorator prints laser-2 after its swap, and the Kotlin class still prints laser-1 when Java swaps it. a == b is false until you add equals and hashCode, then true.

aside.title: Why doesn't the wrapped object call my override?
aside.html: Because it has never heard of your class. With by, the inner object is a separate object, and its own methods call each other directly. So if a set wrapper overrides add, the inner set's addAll still calls the inner add, and your override is skipped. Inheritance works the other way: HashSet.addAll calls add through this, so a subclass's override sees every element. Lesson 5 of the patterns track, Decorator and Proxy, walks through that trap with a map.

sections.h: A delegated property is a hidden field and two calls
sections.html:
Property delegation shares the keyword by and almost nothing else with class delegation. Start without it.

Say every change to an order's status must be logged, and you want the logging written once, in a small helper class you can reuse for any property. By hand, the property forwards its getter and setter to the helper:

Java
final class OrderJava {
    private final Box<String> status = new Box<>("NEW");     // the helper holds the value
    String getStatus() { return status.get(); }
    void setStatus(String s) { status.set("status", s); }    // and logs every change
}
Kotlin
class Order {
    private val statusBox = Audited("NEW")                   // the helper holds the value
    var status: String
        get() = statusBox.getValue(this, ::status)
        set(value) = statusBox.setValue(this, ::status, value)   // and logs every change
}

::status is a reference to the property itself, a KProperty object that knows the property's name. So the helper can log status without a string that could drift out of date. That forwarding is all by does.

In the print shop, it's the cloakroom. The property is your ticket. Reading the property is handing in the ticket to get your coat back, and assigning to it is handing in a coat. The attendant is the helper object: it holds the coat, and it may write each swap in a logbook.

The helper is called the delegate. It needs only two functions with fixed names, getValue and setValue, and then by writes the getter and setter for you:

Java
// Java has no `by`: the helper is an ordinary class, and you write the forwarding above yourself
final class Box<T> {
    private T value;
    Box(T value) { this.value = value; }
    T get() { return value; }
    void set(String name, T value) {
        System.out.println("  " + name + ": " + this.value + " -> " + value);
        this.value = value;
    }
}
Kotlin
class Audited<T>(private var value: T) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> {
    override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value

    override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) {
        println("  ${property.name}: ${this.value} -> $value")
        this.value = value
    }
}

class Order {
    var status: String by Audited("NEW")      // the same forwarding, written by the compiler
    var copies: Long by Audited(0L)
}

getValue receives the owning object (thisRef) and the KProperty, and setValue also gets the new value. A val needs only getValue. You can write the two as operator fun members, as extension functions on any class, or by implementing the standard interfaces ReadOnlyProperty or ReadWriteProperty, as Audited does.

The compiler's version matches the hand-written one with one change, shown in the figure. For each delegated property, it adds a hidden field, status$delegate, typed as whatever the expression after by returns. Instead of building a fresh ::status on every call, it builds one static array per class, $$delegatedProperties, with a KProperty object for each property, filled once when the class is loaded. Then getStatus() loads status$delegate, loads $$delegatedProperties[0], calls getValue, and casts the result to String.

Java sees none of this. It sees getStatus() and setStatus(String), ordinary methods, and the delegate field is private. That suits libraries that work through getters and setters. It's also a warning: a setter that logs or checks looks exactly like a plain setter from the outside.

A few kinds of delegate get no $delegate field: another property (by this::pageCount), a named object, this, or a constant. The docs list the cases. Every other delegated property gets a hidden field in every instance, and usually a new delegate object to put in it.

That's where the cloakroom picture breaks. A real cloakroom has one attendant for everybody. Here, every ticket usually comes with an attendant of its own.

The two operators don't have to live in the delegate's class. They can be extension functions, and that's how by settings works on a plain Map in the last section. The standard library declares getValue as an extension operator on Map that looks up the key property.name. You can do the same for a class you don't own. ResourceBundle is the JDK class that holds an app's texts in one language. With operator fun ResourceBundle.getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): String = getString(property.name), a class can write val greeting: String by messages.

The delegate you'll use most often isn't one you write yourself, though. It's lazy, and it comes with a bill.

code.title: PropertyDelegateDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo import kotlin.properties.ReadWriteProperty import kotlin.reflect.KProperty /** A hand-written delegate: getValue and setValue are all the compiler needs. */ class Audited<T>(private var value: T) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> { override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) { println(" ${property.name}: ${this.value} -> $value") this.value = value } } class Order { var status: String by Audited("NEW") var copies: Long by Audited(0L) } fun main() { val order = Order() order.status = "PRINTING" order.copies = 250 println("status = ${order.status}, copies = ${order.copies}") println("fields the compiler generated:") Order::class.java.declaredFields.forEach { println(" ${it.type.simpleName} ${it.name}") } }

alt.title: PropertyDelegateDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Field; /** * Java twin of PropertyDelegateDemo.kt. Java sees getStatus and setStatus, ordinary methods, * and can't tell that a delegate sits behind them. */ public class PropertyDelegateDemoJava { // the hand-written Java shape: a field holding a helper object, and accessors that call it static final class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } void set(String name, T value) { System.out.println(" " + name + ": " + this.value + " -> " + value); this.value = value; } } static final class OrderJava { private final Box<String> status = new Box<>("NEW"); String getStatus() { return status.get(); } void setStatus(String s) { status.set("status", s); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Order order = new Order(); // the Kotlin class order.setStatus("PRINTING"); // goes through status$delegate.setValue order.setCopies(250L); System.out.println("status = " + order.getStatus() + ", copies = " + order.getCopies()); OrderJava hand = new OrderJava(); hand.setStatus("PRINTING"); System.out.println("fields of the Kotlin Order, seen by reflection:"); for (Field f : Order.class.getDeclaredFields()) { System.out.println(" " + f.getType().getSimpleName() + " " + f.getName()); } } }

Adding note adds a note$delegate field and a third array entry, not a second array.

sections.h: What by lazy costs: objects in every instance and a call on every read
sections.html:
by lazy computes a value the first time someone reads the property, then keeps it. The memory model track took it apart in lesson 5. It is double-checked locking (check, take a lock, check again), and SYNCHRONIZED is the default of its three modes, next to PUBLICATION and NONE. A lock lets only one thread at a time run a piece of code, a thread being one path of execution in the program. Here the lock makes sure that only one thread runs the initializer. This section is about the bill.

In the cloakroom, lazy is the attendant who fetches your item from the stockroom only the first time anybody asks for it, and keeps it at the counter after that.

The demo's PaperSpec looks up how much one sheet of paper weighs, in a paper catalogue that is slow and sometimes times out:

Java
// Java's per-instance lazy field: volatile double-checked locking, by hand
private volatile Double sheetGrams;

double sheetGrams() {
    Double v = sheetGrams;
    if (v == null) {
        synchronized (this) {
            v = sheetGrams;
            if (v == null) sheetGrams = v = catalogue.weightOf("A4 plain");
        }
    }
    return v;
}
Kotlin
class PaperSpec(private val catalogue: PaperCatalogue) {
    val sheetGrams: Double by lazy { catalogue.weightOf("A4 plain") }   // SYNCHRONIZED
}

Each PaperSpec gets a private final kotlin.Lazy sheetGrams$delegate field. The constructor fills it with a new SynchronizedLazyImpl, an object with fields for the initializer, the value and the lock. The initializer lambda is one more object whenever it uses the instance, as this one uses catalogue.

Every read then calls Lazy.getValue() through an interface, and for a Double it also unboxes with checkcast Number and doubleValue. There's no $$delegatedProperties array, because lazy never looks at the property.

For one settings object, none of that matters. For a class you create for every page or every print job, it's two extra objects each time, for a value you may never read. Use lazy on objects that live long: the app's settings, a cache, one shared catalogue. For short-lived ones, compute the value in the constructor, or make it a function.

lazy pays off on objects that live long. On objects you create by the million, compute the value or make it a function.

When only one thread can ever touch the object, lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) drops the lock, and the class becomes UnsafeLazyImpl. The docs say it "doesn't incur any thread-safety guarantees and related overhead". Think of a report builder that lives inside one function call. Don't use it on an object that many threads read at once: NONE gives you no guarantee that they all see one value.

One behavior is easy to miss: lazy has a short memory for failures. It doesn't keep an exception. In the demo, the first read throws paper catalogue timed out, the second read runs the initializer again and succeeds, and only then is the value kept. For a slow lookup, that's usually what you want.

The standard library has more delegates like lazy, ready to use, and one hook that lets a delegate check its property before anyone reads it.

try.title: Count the initializer runs
steps: Run LazyDemo. Before you do, predict how many times the initializer runs over three reads when the first one throws.
Run LazyDemoJava, which does the same with hand-written double-checked locking and then reads the Kotlin class from Java.

code.title: LazyDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo var lookups = 0 class PaperSpec { /** Default mode: SYNCHRONIZED. The first reader runs the initializer under a lock. */ val sheetGrams: Double by lazy { lookups++ if (lookups == 1) throw IllegalStateException("paper catalogue timed out") 4.99 // one A4 sheet of 80 g/m2 paper } } fun main() { for (mode in LazyThreadSafetyMode.entries) { println("$mode -> ${lazy(mode) { 0 }.javaClass.name}") } val spec = PaperSpec() try { spec.sheetGrams } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("first read failed: ${e.message}") } println("second read: ${spec.sheetGrams} (initializer ran $lookups times)") println("third read: ${spec.sheetGrams} (initializer ran $lookups times)") println("field: ${PaperSpec::class.java.declaredFields.joinToString { "${it.type.name} ${it.name}" }}") }

alt.title: LazyDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; /** * Java twin of LazyDemo.kt. Java has no lazy delegate. For a per-instance lazy field the usual * shape is double-checked locking on a volatile field, which is what Kotlin's SYNCHRONIZED mode does. */ public class LazyDemoJava { static int lookups = 0; static final class PaperSpecJava { private volatile Double sheetGrams; // null means "not computed yet" double sheetGrams() { Double v = sheetGrams; if (v == null) { synchronized (this) { v = sheetGrams; if (v == null) { lookups++; if (lookups == 1) throw new IllegalStateException("paper catalogue timed out"); sheetGrams = v = 4.99; } } } return v; } } public static void main(String[] args) { PaperSpecJava spec = new PaperSpecJava(); try { spec.sheetGrams(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("first read failed: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("second read: " + spec.sheetGrams() + " (initializer ran " + lookups + " times)"); System.out.println("third read: " + spec.sheetGrams() + " (initializer ran " + lookups + " times)"); // the Kotlin class from Java: getSheetGrams() calls Lazy.getValue() on every read PaperSpec kotlinSpec = new PaperSpec(); try { kotlinSpec.getSheetGrams(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("Kotlin PaperSpec from Java, first read failed: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("Kotlin PaperSpec from Java, second read: " + kotlinSpec.getSheetGrams()); } }

try.expect: The three modes map to kotlin.SynchronizedLazyImpl, kotlin.SafePublicationLazyImpl and kotlin.UnsafeLazyImpl. The first read fails with paper catalogue timed out, the second returns 4.99, and the initializer ran 2 times, not 3: once the value is kept, reads stop calling it. The only field is kotlin.Lazy sheetGrams$delegate, and getSheetGrams is getfield, invokeinterface Lazy.getValue, checkcast Number, doubleValue. The Java version behaves the same.

sections.h: The standard delegates, and provideDelegate for early checks
sections.html:
The standard library ships the delegates you'd otherwise write by hand. Delegates.observable(initial) { property, old, new -> } calls you after every assignment. Delegates.vetoable(initial) { property, old, new -> Boolean } calls you before it, and returning false keeps the old value. In the cloakroom, the first is the attendant who notes every swap in the logbook. The second looks at what you hand in, and may refuse it.

A val can also read from a Map: val host: String by settings looks up the key "host", like an attendant who finds your coat on a rack by the name on your ticket. A var does the same with a MutableMap.

Delegates.notNull<Int>() covers what lateinit can't. (lateinit marks a var that gets its first value after construction, and it doesn't work for primitive types such as Int.) Reading a notNull property before the first assignment throws Property size should be initialized before get.

Here are the first three, by hand in Java and with delegates in Kotlin:

Java
void setOwner(String owner) {                          // observable, by hand
    String old = this.owner;
    this.owner = owner;
    System.out.println("owner: " + old + " -> " + owner);
}

void setCopies(int copies) {                           // vetoable, by hand
    if (copies <= 100) this.copies = copies;
}

int port() { return (Integer) settings.get("port"); }  // map-backed, by hand
Kotlin
var owner: String by Delegates.observable("<none>") { property, old, new ->
    println("${property.name}: $old -> $new")
}
var copies: Int by Delegates.vetoable(1) { _, _, new -> new <= 100 }

val port: Int by settings                              // settings["port"], cast to Int

The demo prints owner: <none> -> alice, owner: alice -> bob, copies after veto: 1 and copies after ok: 50. The shop's limit of 100 copies per request turned the 500 away.

A map-backed property fails only when you read it. A missing key throws java.util.NoSuchElementException: Key port is missing in the map. That's late. For settings, you'd rather fail when the object is built, and that's what provideDelegate is for.

If the object after by has an operator fun provideDelegate(thisRef, property), the compiler calls it once per property, while the owning object is being constructed. Then it keeps whatever provideDelegate returns as the real delegate. The docs describe it as the way to get "the necessary validation right away", and PropertyDelegateProvider { thisRef, property -> ... } creates one without writing a new class.

In the cloakroom, it's the attendant who checks your ticket as you walk in, not when you come back for your coat. In the demo, binding printerHost prints during ShopSettings(), before anyone reads the property. The lab uses the same trick to register every recorded property up front.

Check settings when the object is built, not when they're first read. provideDelegate is the hook for it.

Every delegate here adds a hidden field to each instance, usually holding one more object, and puts logic behind a getter or setter that looks plain from the outside. In the lab, you'll write a delegate that earns both: a recorder that logs every real change to a print job.

Remove "host" to "laser-1.local" from the map. Predict which line fails, and when.

code.title: StdDelegatesDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo import kotlin.properties.Delegates import kotlin.properties.PropertyDelegateProvider import kotlin.properties.ReadOnlyProperty class PrintRequest { // observable: the handler runs after the assignment var owner: String by Delegates.observable("<none>") { property, old, new -> println("${property.name}: $old -> $new") } // vetoable: the handler runs before the assignment; false keeps the old value var copies: Int by Delegates.vetoable(1) { _, _, new -> new <= 100 } } class PrinterConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val host: String by settings // reads settings["host"] val port: Int by settings // reads settings["port"] } /** provideDelegate runs once per property, while the object is built: validation happens right away. */ fun requiredSetting(): PropertyDelegateProvider<Any?, ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, String>> = PropertyDelegateProvider { _, property -> println("binding ${property.name}") ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> "value of ${property.name}" } } class ShopSettings { val printerHost: String by requiredSetting() } fun main() { val request = PrintRequest() request.owner = "alice" request.owner = "bob" request.copies = 500 println("copies after veto: ${request.copies}") request.copies = 50 println("copies after ok: ${request.copies}") val config = PrinterConfig(mapOf("host" to "laser-1.local")) println("host = ${config.host}") try { println("port = ${config.port}") } catch (e: NoSuchElementException) { println("port failed on access: ${e.message}") } println("building ShopSettings...") val s = ShopSettings() println("built; printerHost = ${s.printerHost}") }

alt.title: StdDelegatesDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; import java.util.Map; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; /** * Java twin of StdDelegatesDemo.kt. Java writes each behavior into the setter or getter by hand. */ public class StdDelegatesDemoJava { static final class PrintRequestJava { private String owner = "<none>"; private int copies = 1; void setOwner(String owner) { String old = this.owner; this.owner = owner; // observable: assign, then notify System.out.println("owner: " + old + " -> " + owner); } void setCopies(int copies) { if (copies <= 100) this.copies = copies; // vetoable: check, then assign } int getCopies() { return copies; } } static final class PrinterConfigJava { private final Map<String, Object> settings; PrinterConfigJava(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.settings = settings; } String host() { return (String) get("host"); } int port() { return (Integer) get("port"); } private Object get(String key) { if (!settings.containsKey(key)) throw new NoSuchElementException("Key " + key + " is missing in the map."); return settings.get(key); } } // provideDelegate has no Java twin: Java validates in the constructor, which also runs at build time static final class ShopSettingsJava { final String printerHost; ShopSettingsJava() { System.out.println("binding printerHost"); printerHost = "value of printerHost"; } } public static void main(String[] args) { PrintRequestJava request = new PrintRequestJava(); request.setOwner("alice"); request.setOwner("bob"); request.setCopies(500); System.out.println("copies after veto: " + request.getCopies()); request.setCopies(50); System.out.println("copies after ok: " + request.getCopies()); PrinterConfigJava config = new PrinterConfigJava(Map.of("host", "laser-1.local")); System.out.println("host = " + config.host()); try { System.out.println("port = " + config.port()); } catch (NoSuchElementException e) { System.out.println("port failed on access: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("building ShopSettings..."); ShopSettingsJava s = new ShopSettingsJava(); System.out.println("built; printerHost = " + s.printerHost); } }

try.expect: building ShopSettings... comes first, then binding printerHost while the constructor runs, then built; printerHost = value of printerHost. With new <= 40 both assignments are vetoed, so both lines print 1: the handler checks assignments, never the initial value. Without host, building PrinterConfig still works, and the program fails on the config.host read with Key host is missing in the map.

compare.title: An audited field: Java setters vs a Kotlin delegate

java.title: PrintJob.java
java.html: public final class PrintJob { private final ChangeLog log; private String status = "NEW"; private int copies = 1; public PrintJob(ChangeLog log) { this.log = log; } public String getStatus() { return status; } public void setStatus(String s) { if (!s.equals(status)) log.record("status", status, s); // repeated in every setter status = s; } public int getCopies() { return copies; } public void setCopies(int c) { if (c != copies) log.record("copies", copies, c); copies = c; } }

kotlin.title: PrintJob.kt
kotlin.html: class Recorded<T>(private var value: T, private val log: ChangeLog) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> { override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) { if (value != this.value) log.changes += Change(property.name, this.value, value) this.value = value } } class PrintJob(val log: ChangeLog) { var status: String by Recorded("NEW", log) // the audit is written once, in Recorded var copies: Int by Recorded(1, log) }

compare.note: Both record every real change to a print job, so the shop can see who changed what. In Java the record lives in every setter, and a new field without it is a silent gap that only a careful reviewer can catch. In Kotlin it's written once, in the delegate, and each property opts in with by. The property name comes from the KProperty the compiler passes in, so it can't drift from the field name the way a string literal can. The run-time price is one delegate object per property per instance, plus one static KProperty array per class. Java code calling the Kotlin class can't tell the two apart: it sees getStatus and setStatus either way.

worked.title: A config object that fails at start-up, not on the first job

steps.say: Start with a map-backed config for the shop's app. It reads nicely, but a missing key is found only when someone reads the property, which may be the first job sent to that printer, late at night.
steps.code: final class ShopConfig { private final Map<String, Object> settings; ShopConfig(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.settings = settings; } String printerHost() { return (String) settings.get("printerHost"); } // null if missing long timeoutMs() { return (Long) settings.get("timeoutMs"); } // NullPointerException if missing }

alt.html: class ShopConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val printerHost: String by settings // NoSuchElementException, but only when read val timeoutMs: Long by settings }

steps.say: Write a provider. provideDelegate runs once per property while the object is built, so it can check the key right away and hand back a delegate that only returns the value it read.
steps.code: fun <T> Map<String, Any?>.required(): PropertyDelegateProvider<Any?, ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, T>> = PropertyDelegateProvider { _, property -> // 1. check the key while the owning object is constructed require(property.name in this) { "missing config key '${property.name}'" } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val value = this[property.name] as T // 2. the real delegate just returns what was read ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> value } } class ShopConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val printerHost: String by settings.required() val timeoutMs: Long by settings.required() }

alt.html: // Java does the same check in the constructor, one line per key ShopConfig(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.printerHost = (String) require(settings, "printerHost"); this.timeoutMs = (Long) require(settings, "timeoutMs"); } private static Object require(Map<String, Object> m, String key) { if (!m.containsKey(key)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing config key '" + key + "'"); return m.get(key); }

steps.say: Build one with a key missing. It fails in the constructor, with the property's name in the message, because the name came from the KProperty the compiler passed in.
steps.code: ShopConfig(mapOf("printerHost" to "laser-1.local", "timeoutMs" to 2_000L)) // fine ShopConfig(mapOf("printerHost" to "laser-1.local")) // java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: missing config key 'timeoutMs'

alt.html: new ShopConfig(Map.of("printerHost", "laser-1.local", "timeoutMs", 2_000L)); // fine new ShopConfig(Map.of("printerHost", "laser-1.local")); // java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: missing config key 'timeoutMs'

steps.say: The cast is still unchecked: a "timeoutMs" to "2000" entry passes the check and fails later, with a ClassCastException on the first read. If that matters, pass the expected class into required and check it with isInstance, the class-token trick from the generics track.

lab.title: An audited property delegate
steps: A PrintJob is a job being prepared at the counter, and its ChangeLog records every real change to it. Run the tests. All six fail, most with NotImplementedError thrown while a PrintJob is being built. That's provideDelegate at work already.
In Recorded.kt, write getValue and setValue (TODOs 1 and 2). Record a Change only when the value really changes.
Write ChangeLog.recorded (TODO 3): return a PropertyDelegateProvider that checks and registers property.name, then creates the Recorded.
In PrintJob.kt, make paperSize a vetoable delegate (TODO 4), and delegate both PrinterProfile properties to the map (TODO 5).

Run the tests until all six pass, including JobFromJavaTest, which only sees setStatus, setCopies and getLog. Then run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/main workbench.kotlin.l03.PrintJob and match each field to a property.
hints: In setValue, the parameter value shadows the field. Compare with if (value != this.value), record Change(property.name, this.value, value), then assign this.value = value.
PropertyDelegateProvider { _, property -> check(property.name !in tracked) { "..." }; tracked += property.name; Recorded(initial, this) }. Inside the lambda, this is still the ChangeLog receiver.
var paperSize: String by Delegates.vetoable("A4") { _, _, new -> new.matches(Regex("A[0-6]")) }, with import kotlin.properties.Delegates.
val name: String by settings needs no import. Delete the get() = TODO(...) and write by settings in its place.
lab.done: All six tests in DelegationTest and JobFromJavaTest pass.

drill.title: Write a clamping delegate from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class Clamped(min: Int, max: Int, initial: Int) as a ReadWriteProperty<Any?, Int> that keeps every assigned value inside min..max, and use it as var copies: Int by Clamped(1, 100, initial = 1). Then write the Java setter that does the same. What does copies = 500 leave behind?

answer.html: class Clamped(private val min: Int, private val max: Int, initial: Int) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, Int> { private var value = initial.coerceIn(min, max) override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): Int = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: Int) { this.value = value.coerceIn(min, max) } } class PrintRequest { var copies: Int by Clamped(1, 100, initial = 1) // 500 is stored as 100 }

alt.title: PrintRequest.java
alt.html: final class PrintRequest { private int copies = 1; int getCopies() { return copies; } void setCopies(int c) { copies = Math.max(1, Math.min(100, c)); // 500 is stored as 100 } }

recap: Class delegation (: Iface by x) forwards every interface method you don't override to x, captured once into a hidden final $$delegate_0 field. Reassigning a var doesn't move it.
equals, hashCode and toString are not forwarded, and the delegate never calls back into your overrides.
A delegated property compiles to a prop$delegate field, a static $$delegatedProperties array of KProperty objects, and accessors that call getValue and setValue. Java sees plain getters and setters.

by lazy costs a Lazy object (and an initializer lambda that uses the instance) per instance, plus an interface call on every read. It doesn't keep exceptions. Use NONE only for objects one thread uses.
observable runs after an assignment, vetoable before it, by map reads a key named after the property when you read it, and provideDelegate runs once per property while the object is built.

The limit: every delegated property adds a hidden field to each instance, usually holding its own delegate object, and its logic hides behind getters and setters that look plain from Java and from the call site.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks what the compiler actually generates for var status: String by log.recorded("NEW") in PrintJob, and what a Java caller sees when it calls setStatus. Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: log.recorded("NEW") returns a delegate provider, so while the PrintJob is being constructed the compiler calls its provideDelegate with the property's KProperty, and stores the Recorded it returns in a hidden private field called status$delegate. The class also gets one static array, $$delegatedProperties, holding a KProperty for each delegated property. The getter getStatus() loads the delegate and the matching KProperty and calls getValue, then casts the result to String. The setter calls setValue(this, property, value), which is where Recorded compares the old and new value and writes a change to the log. A Java caller sees nothing special: just a public setStatus(String) method. It can't tell there's a delegate behind it, but the change is still recorded, because the logic lives in the setter the compiler generated.

deeper.html:
Delegating to another property is the one case worth knowing that has no $delegate field at all. It is useful when you rename a property and need the old name for a while:

Java
// Java keeps the old accessor by hand and marks it deprecated
public int getPageCount() { return pageCount; }
@Deprecated public int getPages() { return pageCount; }
Kotlin
class PrintJob {
    var pageCount: Int = 0

    @Deprecated("Use pageCount", ReplaceWith("pageCount"))
    var pages: Int by this::pageCount
}

javap -p on that class shows getPages and setPages, a private static helper getPages$delegate(PrintJob), and no pages$delegate field: the accessors read and write pageCount directly. The IDE offers the ReplaceWith fix at every call site, so the rename can finish over a few releases.

The other cases without a field, from the docs: a delegate that is a named object, this, a constant expression or an enum entry, and "a final val property with a backing field and a default getter in the same module". Everything else pays for a hidden field, and usually a delegate object, per property per instance.

One more design note on class delegation, after the aside in the first section. The delegate never calling back into your class can look like a flaw, but it is also what makes by predictable. A subclass of HashSet depends on how HashSet calls its own methods, which a future JDK may change. A by wrapper depends only on the interface, so it behaves the same whatever the inner class does inside.
